content.text: A method call either returns or throws, and it's fast enough to ignore. A call to another service over HTTP can also end with no answer at all, and then you don't know whether the work happened. Latency adds up, and failures multiply along chains of calls. Design every remote call for three outcomes, with a deadline, and with an answer for "I don't know".

Support forwards a complaint: a customer was charged twice for one order. The logs show that checkout's call to the payments service timed out, the page said "Payment failed, please try again", and she clicked again. Both charges went through. Before the team split out payments, that line was
payments.Charge(order)
. Now it's an
await
on an HTTP call, and the code around it never changed, because it looked like the same call.
The common misconception
The belief: calling another service over HTTP is just like calling a method, only a little slower. You wrap it in an interface, inject it,
await
it, and handle exceptions the way you always do.
Smart developers believe it because the tooling makes it look true. A generated client gives you typed methods, an
IPaymentsClient

interface looks like any in-process service, and on a laptop the other service runs on localhost and answers in milliseconds, every time. Microsoft's microservices guide describes the trap: in a monolith, components call each other with method calls, and "A direct conversion from in-process method calls into RPC calls to services will cause a chatty and not efficient communication that won't perform well in distributed environments."

The idea is old, too. Around the turn of the century, distributed object middleware promised that you could call an object without caring whether it lived in your process or on another machine. Martin Fowler's verdict on it: "you can't encapsulate the remote/in-process distinction."
What actually happens
A remote call has a third outcome

Fowler spells out the difference: "An in-process function call is fast and always succeeds (in that any exceptions are due to the application, not due to the mere fact of making the call). Remote calls, however, are orders of magnitude slower, and there's always a chance that the call will fail due to a failure in the remote process or the connection."

The worst case isn't a clear failure. It's a timeout. When no response arrives, any of these may be true: the request never reached the server, the server did the work and the response was lost, or the server is still working. That's
partial failure
, and the caller can't tell which one happened. Treat "no answer" as "no" and you charge twice. Treat it as "yes" and you ship unpaid orders.
Latency adds up

A method call costs nanoseconds, so nobody counts them. A remote call costs a network round trip plus serialization, and APIs designed for in-process use make many small calls. Fowler's example: in process, you can happily ask for 100 product prices with 100 calls; remotely, "you're usually better off to batch all that into a single call that asks for all 100 prices and availabilities in one go." The interface has to change shape, not just get slower.
Chains make it worse. Microsoft's guide: "The more you add synchronous dependencies between microservices, such as query requests, the worse the overall response time gets for the client apps."
Failures multiply along a chain

If serving a request needs three other services to answer synchronously, it fails whenever any of them is down or slow. Microsoft is direct: if one microservice must call others to answer a client, "you have an architecture that won't be resilient when some microservices fail." Slow is often worse than down, because waiting holds resources: "Timeouts that are too long cause threads and connections to accumulate during outages."
The eight fallacies

Peter Deutsch's list, as James Gosling's site publishes it, begins: "Essentially everyone, when they first build a distributed application, makes the following eight assumptions. All prove to be false in the long run and all cause big trouble and painful learning experiences." The
fallacies
Fowler calls this list "the classic statement of why one should beware of any notion that distribution can be done transparently (or easily)." The double charge above breaks the first two at once.
The fix: design for three outcomes

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: The fixed version admits what the network can't promise. The call has a deadline, so a slow payments service can't hold the request forever. A 4xx means Payments answered and didn't charge. A 5xx or no answer means "unknown", and checkout shows "We're confirming your payment" instead of "try again". Because the caller creates the charge's
Id
, the unknown case can be resolved by asking Payments about it instead of charging again. Retrying is one possible next step, with risks covered later in this path; how to hold the
HttpClient
itself is covered in the article on
IHttpClientFactory

A retry turns an unknown into a possible duplicate. Microsoft's guidance warns that "If an application repeats parts of a multistep process and the operations aren't idempotent, inconsistencies can occur", and that retries stacked at several layers multiply: three retries at two levels add up to nine attempts against the service. Retries need their own design, not a loop around the call.

blocks.title: Give every outbound call a deadline

content.text: Microsoft's advice is to "Set timeouts on every outbound call before you implement retry logic." Derive the deadline from what the user is waiting for: if checkout must answer within five seconds, a payment call can't be allowed to take 30.

The list is credited to L. Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems, and it's often said that James Gosling added the eighth. In a 2021 interview, Deutsch recalled that the first four were already known at Sun when he arrived, that he added the next four, and that a presentation he gave there had all eight.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find the calls that cross the network

content.text: Search for
HttpClient
, gRPC clients and generated API clients, including the ones hidden behind interfaces like
IPaymentsClient
. List every call a request makes.
Set a timeout per call that fits the end-to-end time the caller allows, and pass the request's cancellation token along.

items.title: Decide what "unknown" means for each write

content.text: For every call that changes something, write down what happens when there's no answer: check status by ID, show a pending state, or reconcile later.
Replace loops of small remote calls with one call that sends or returns the whole set, and question every synchronous chain longer than one hop.
Key takeaways

items.text: A network call can succeed, fail, or leave you not knowing; design every remote call for all three.
A timeout doesn't mean the work didn't happen, so don't treat "no answer" as "no".
Remote calls cost a round trip each, so APIs must be coarse-grained, not chatty.
Synchronous chains add up latency and multiply the chance that something on the path fails.
The eight fallacies are a checklist of what the network won't do for you; check your design against them.
